title: A Simple, Two-Paragraph Template that Helps Kids to Really Argue
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart explains why he requires students to answer each argumentative Article of the Week with a two-paragraph They Say, I Say template adapted from Graff and Birkenstein. He argues that teenagers are passionate arguers outside school but lack the tools to enter academic, professional or civic conversations, so scaffolding is warranted. The template forces students to identify an author's general argument, build on it, state and illustrate a claim, and anticipate a naysayer. He defends the constraint with a Karate Kid analogy, jacket on and jacket off, in which repetitive structure trains deeper skill. In-class debates provide the payoff that motivates the writing work.
points: Students need scaffolding to move from everyday argument to academic argument, and a fixed template supplies it.
The first sentence of the template reveals at once whether a student understood the author's general argument.
Real argument builds on others' ideas, which is why the whole first paragraph is devoted to summarizing the other side.
Predicting a naysayer's response is a core argumentative habit that the template makes explicit.
Short in-class debates give students a reason to want the discipline of structured writing.
quotes: The problem with joining in on the conversation is that, although my teenage students (like yours) are passionate arguers in whatever topics they like to nerd out about outside of school — sports, fashion, video games, anime, or whatever — they often lack the tools for entering into argumentative conversations in academic, professional, or civic realms.
Get this: I'm requiring that every student use this template until I see they've fully internalized the moves it contains.
True argument involves building off the ideas of others; it's not simply spouting off your opinion and, if you're really snazzy, giving a cursory mention of what someone else said.

Effective arguers naturally predict what a naysayer might say. Ironically, some are concerned that the Common Core's emphasis on argument is going to create a more fragmented society, but I would argue that nothing is better than argument at helping people to see any given issue from a myriad of sides. I'm not aiming for pithiness when I say that real argument drives people together; I see it in my classroom every year.

This template, in its first sentence, allows me to see if they've got the general argument pinned. It also helps them internalize that the general argument is what an effective arguer focuses on — not debatable side points.

These argumentative events help my students experience how the moves in the They Say / I Say two-paragraph template makes for a more cohesive, entertaining, rigorous debate experience, and that whets their appetite for doing the hard work in writing arguments.
